details:
**"The horror! The horror!"**
The famous last words of Kurtz, whispered as he dies aboard Marlow's steamer heading back down the Congo River. This is the most common giveaway.

**"Exterminate all the brutes!"**
The scrawled postscript at the end of Kurtz's eloquent seventeen-page report for the International Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs. The report is full of high-minded talk of civilizing Africans, and the postscript reveals what lies beneath it. Marlow later hands the report over with the postscript torn off.

**Mr. Kurtz**
The Company's most successful ivory trader, a "universal genius" (painter, musician, writer) who runs the remote Inner Station. He has made himself a god among the local people and has fallen into savagery. Marlow is sent to retrieve him, and Kurtz dies on the voyage back.

**Charles Marlow**
The narrator of the inner story, a seaman who as a child loved the "blank spaces" on maps and was "charmed" by the snake-like river on a map of Africa. With help from his aunt, he gets a job with the Company as captain of a river steamboat. Conrad also used Marlow as the narrator of Lord Jim.

**The Nellie and the Thames frame story**
The novella opens on the Nellie, a "cruising yawl" anchored in the Thames, where Marlow, sitting "in the pose of a meditating Buddha," tells his story to friends. He imagines Roman soldiers arriving in Britain at "the very end of the world" and says, "this also has been one of the dark places of the earth." It ends when the Director of Companies says, "We have lost the first of the ebb," and the narrator sees a black bank of clouds over the river.

**The Intended**
Kurtz's fiancee in Brussels, whom Marlow visits at the end. When she asks for Kurtz's last words, Marlow lies and says they were her name, rather than "The horror! The horror!"

**The Russian "Harlequin"**
A young Russian trader in a patchwork suit of many colors who worships Kurtz and repeats that Kurtz has "enlarged my mind." His copy of An Inquiry into Some Points of Seamanship by Tower, Towson contains notes in Russian that Marlow mistakes for code. He leaves a note on a woodpile: "Hurry up. Approach cautiously."

**The "whited sepulchre," the knitting women, and the doctor**
Marlow calls the Company's European city (Brussels) a "whited sepulchre," borrowing Jesus's image of hypocrisy from Matthew. In the Company's office, two women knit black wool like Fates guarding the door of Darkness. A company doctor measures Marlow's skull, notes that "the changes take place inside," and warns him to avoid exposure to the sun.

**Fresleven and the two black hens**
Marlow's predecessor, a Danish captain described as "the gentlest, quietest creature." He was killed in a quarrel over two black hens after beating a village chief, and his death creates the vacancy that Marlow fills.

**Kurtz's painting of a blindfolded woman with a torch**
At the Central Station, Marlow sees a small oil sketch by Kurtz of a draped, blindfolded woman carrying a lighted torch against a dark background. It is in the room of the brickmaker, a scheming agent whom Marlow calls a "papier-mache Mephistopheles."

**The Central Station and the rivets**
At the Central Station, Marlow finds his steamboat sunk and waits months for rivets to repair it, while the Manager seems to want Kurtz to fail. On the way there, at the Outer Station, he meets the immaculately dressed Chief Accountant, who complains that a dying agent's groans distract him from his books, and he sees a chain gang of starving workers. The Eldorado Exploring Expedition passes through, and all that is later heard of it is that "all the donkeys were dead."

**The attack on the steamer and the helmsman's death**
Near the Inner Station, natives attack the steamer at Kurtz's order. The African helmsman is killed by a spear, and Marlow throws his own blood-filled shoes overboard, then the helmsman's body. A fat "pilgrim" in pink pyjamas takes the wheel. Earlier, Marlow is amazed that the starving cannibal crew, whose rotten hippo meat was thrown overboard, do not attack the whites.

**The heads on stakes and Kurtz's mistress**
Kurtz's hut at the Inner Station is surrounded by posts topped with the shrunken heads of "rebels." A tall, magnificent African woman, apparently Kurtz's mistress, appears on the shore with her hair done up in the shape of a helmet and stands defiantly as the steamer leaves.

**Chinua Achebe's "An Image of Africa"**
Achebe's 1975 lecture, which famously called Conrad "a bloody racist" (later revised to "a thoroughgoing racist"). It argues that the novella portrays Africa as "the other world" and denies Africans human expression.

**"Mistah Kurtz—he dead," The Hollow Men, and Apocalypse Now**
The manager's servant announces Kurtz's death contemptuously with the line "Mistah Kurtz—he dead," which T. S. Eliot used as the epigraph of "The Hollow Men." Francis Ford Coppola adapted the story as the Vietnam War film Apocalypse Now (1979), with Martin Sheen as Captain Willard and Marlon Brando as Colonel Kurtz.
